# Visualising a time series {#sec-visualising}

The first step in any forecasting task is to plot the data. A time plot shows
the observations against time and makes the trend and seasonality easy to see.

```{r}
#| label: fig-passengers
#| fig-cap: "Monthly international airline passengers, 1949–1960."
#| message: false
library(ggplot2)

# Turn the monthly series into a data frame for plotting
passengers <- data.frame(
  month = seq(as.Date("1949-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = length(AirPassengers)),
  count = as.numeric(AirPassengers)
)

ggplot(passengers, aes(x = month, y = count)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Airline passengers",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Passengers (thousands)"
  )
```

@fig-passengers shows a clear upward trend. The seasonal pattern also grows
with the level of the series: the summer peaks become larger every year.

## Seasonal plots {#sec-seasonal-plots}

A seasonal plot draws each year as a separate line, so that the shape of the
seasonal pattern is easier to compare from one year to the next.

```{r}
#| label: fig-seasonal
#| fig-cap: "Each year of the series drawn as its own line."
# One line per year, coloured from earliest to latest
passengers$year <- format(passengers$month, "%Y")
passengers$month_of_year <- as.integer(format(passengers$month, "%m"))

ggplot(passengers, aes(x = month_of_year, y = count, group = year, colour = year)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb) +
  labs(x = "Month of the year", y = "Passengers (thousands)", colour = "Year")
```

July and August are the busiest months in every year of the data.
